problem: Prior LLM-for-robotics work relies on predefined simulator-specific API functions or free-form generated code, which can be buggy or unsafe and does not transfer across robots, so natural language cannot be reliably turned into executable, real-world mobile-robot plans.
motivation: Robots need to translate natural language (text or voice) into physically feasible action sequences. LLM-generated code can drift and drive robots into invalid states, so grounding the LLM in a fixed, reliable library of robot functions is proposed as a safer route to human-level planning.
key_idea: Wrap navigation (RL-based), AR-marker localization, and pick/place modules as ROS API functions in a library, and let any LLM (GPT-4 here) zero-shot compose them into executable robot programs from text or voice commands.
insight: The paper is a system contribution. It shows that a fixed, documented function library lets a frozen LLM produce working plans, with over 70% success on all tasks in 50 simulated runs for both chatbot and voicebot. Voice input roughly doubles LLM processing time because of speech-to-text, while robot execution time is unchanged. Among the RL algorithms compared, PPO gave the highest episodic reward, and its policy transferred from Gazebo to the real robot. No ablations isolate the value of the library design.
method: ROS robot library suite: modular API-wise control functions (navigation, Approach/Leave, pick/place, get_position) that the LLM calls instead of writing low-level code

RL navigation: model-free RL (PPO best; also TRPO, VPG, DDPG, TD3) in Gazebo with a 180° lidar state plus heading and goal distance, one-dimensional angular-velocity action (discrete or continuous), reward 5*r_yaw*2^(Dg/Dc) with collision/goal terminal terms
AR-marker localization: ar_track_alvar with ArUco markers gives continuous pose estimates and drives Approach(x)/Leave(x) velocities to a set distance from the pick/place location
Pick & place: MoveIt (OMPL) move_group plans collision-free arm trajectories on the OpenManipulator-X, using the marker alignment
LLM interface: GPT-4 via the OpenAI API, given a prompt describing the library functions, translates text or voice commands into function-call code zero-shot; prompt refined on the first 30 samples
Sim-to-real transfer: the best PPO policy trained in simulation is deployed on a Turtlebot3 in a SLAM-mapped 4x3 m room

setting.backbone: GPT-4 (frozen, zero-shot planner) + PPO RL navigation policy (trained in Gazebo)
setting.training_data: LLM: none (zero-shot prompting); RL navigation policy trained in Gazebo, 250 epochs x 3000 interactions
setting.observation: 2D lidar (180°, -90° to 90°), RGB camera for ArUco markers, wheel encoders, SLAM map, text or voice commands
setting.action_space: angular velocity (discrete or continuous) at constant linear velocity; high-level API function calls; MoveIt arm trajectories
setting.simulator: Gazebo 7.7 + ROS Kinetic (Turtlebot3 Waffle Pi + OpenManipulator-X)
setting.privileged: ArUco fiducial markers placed at pick/place locations, a pre-built SLAM map, and known goal coordinates from get_position

numbers_note: No standard benchmark numbers. Results are given only in figures (per-task time bars, CDFs, and learning curves), with a text statement of success rates over 70% across all tasks.
results: In a home-service scenario (fetch water for an elderly person), 50 simulated runs each for a chatbot and a voicebot interface achieved over 70% success on all tasks. The voicebot's LLM processing time was about double the chatbot's, while robot execution time was comparable. The PPO policy transferred to a real Turtlebot3, which completed the pick-and-place delivery. No baseline systems are compared.
limitations: Evaluation is a single self-designed scenario in a small 4x3 m room, with no comparison to other frameworks or standard benchmarks and only figure-based results
Assumes clear, unambiguous commands, a structured static environment, and fiducial markers for localization
Sim-to-real transfer is shown only qualitatively, and adapting to other robots requires manual fine-tuning
